promptText: What problem does reranking solve that pure vector similarity search alone does not?
options: It expands the set of documents the vector index can search over

It re-scores a small candidate set with a model that reasons jointly about the query and each document, correcting cases where a topically similar but non-answering chunk outranked the chunk that actually answers the question
It eliminates the need for chunking documents before indexing
It replaces the embedding model used for the initial retrieval step
explanation: Bi-encoder similarity is computed from independently-created embeddings and is only approximately correlated with true relevance; reranking uses a jointly-reasoning model on the already-retrieved candidate set to fix ordering errors within it.

promptText: Why can't a cross-encoder be used as the primary retrieval mechanism over an entire corpus of millions of documents?
options: Cross-encoders cannot process text longer than a single sentence

A cross-encoder must process the query and each candidate jointly in a single forward pass with nothing precomputable ahead of time, so scoring millions of documents per query would require millions of full Transformer forward passes — computationally infeasible at that scale
Cross-encoders only work with sparse vectors, not the dense vectors used in retrieval
Cross-encoders require a GPU cluster that costs more than a vector database license
explanation: Bi-encoder embeddings can be precomputed offline and compared cheaply at query time, which is why they scale to full-corpus retrieval, while cross-encoders are reserved for reranking a much smaller, already-narrowed candidate set.

promptText: Architecturally, what is the key difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
options: A bi-encoder uses two separate GPUs while a cross-encoder uses one

A bi-encoder maps the query and document into vectors independently and compares them afterward with a cheap operation; a cross-encoder concatenates query and document into one input and lets self-attention model interactions between every query and document token jointly, producing a single relevance score
A cross-encoder can only be trained on labeled click data, while a bi-encoder cannot
A bi-encoder always outperforms a cross-encoder on relevance judgment
explanation: The bi-encoder's document vector never depends on the query and can be precomputed; the cross-encoder's joint representation captures fine-grained interactions a bi-encoder cannot see, but must be recomputed fresh for every query-document pair.

promptText: Why should you over-fetch a wide candidate set (e.g., top-50) at retrieval time before running a reranker, rather than reranking only the final desired top-5?
options: Reranking APIs require a minimum batch size of 50 candidates to function at all
Reranking can only reorder candidates it is given — it cannot recover a relevant chunk that retrieval excluded entirely, so a narrow initial candidate set defeats the purpose of reranking
Wider candidate sets always reduce reranking latency
Vector databases cannot return fewer than 50 results per query
explanation: If the correct chunk ranked, say, 12th by embedding similarity but retrieval already truncated to top-5, the reranker never sees it and cannot fix the omission — this is the single most common way teams 'add reranking' and see zero improvement.

promptText: Why can't reranker relevance scores generally be cached the way embeddings are?
options: Caching infrastructure for reranking scores does not exist in any cloud provider

A reranker score is a joint function of a specific query and a specific document computed fresh at request time, unlike an embedding which is a query-independent property of a document computed once and reused across future queries
Reranker scores change randomly every time regardless of input, so caching would return wrong answers
Reranking always uses a different candidate set on every call, making caching meaningless
explanation: The whole point of a cross-encoder is that its representation depends jointly on both the query and document, so there is no way to precompute or reuse the score for a different query; only an exact repeat of the same (query, candidates) pair can be cached.

promptText: Why is it inaccurate to say 'the reranker improves recall'?
options: Reranking cannot improve any retrieval quality metric at all

Reranking only reorders a candidate set that retrieval already produced and cannot add a document retrieval never fetched; what it improves is precision within the recall the first stage already achieved
Recall and reranking are unrelated concepts that should never be discussed together
Reranking always decreases recall as a side effect of its computation
explanation: Recall is bounded entirely by stage-1 retrieval; the reranker's job is to move a relevant document that was already present but buried low up to where it will actually be used, which is a precision improvement, not a recall improvement.

promptText: A team reports that adding reranking to their RAG pipeline produced zero measurable improvement. Investigation reveals stage-1 retrieval was only ever configured to return the top-5 candidates before reranking runs. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The reranker model itself must be broken or miscalibrated

Reranking a candidate set that was already truncated too aggressively at retrieval time gives the reranker nothing meaningful to work with — this is the single most common way teams 'add reranking' and see no improvement, then wrongly conclude reranking doesn't work for their use case
This proves reranking never provides value for any RAG system
The embedding model must be swapped before reranking can have any effect
explanation: Reranking requires a genuinely wide candidate pool (commonly top-25 to top-100) to have raw material to correct ordering errors; reranking an already-narrow top-5 defeats the purpose entirely.

promptText: Why should a production reranking pipeline apply an absolute relevance-score floor in addition to top-k truncation?
options: Score floors are required by most reranking API terms of service

A reranker's job is relative ordering among what it was given — it will happily identify the 'best' of several genuinely irrelevant candidates unless an absolute threshold is also checked, so the system can recognize 'I don't have a good answer' for out-of-domain questions
Score floors reduce the latency of the reranking API call
Top-k truncation alone always guarantees relevant results, making a floor purely redundant
explanation: Without an absolute score threshold, a system with no genuinely relevant candidates will still confidently feed the LLM the least-bad of several bad options rather than recognizing it lacks a good answer.

promptText: How does ColBERT-style late interaction sit between bi-encoders and full cross-encoders?
options: It is architecturally identical to a cross-encoder but runs on a smaller model

It represents documents as per-token vectors that are precomputable offline like a bi-encoder, then applies a query-time MaxSim operation approximating token-level matching without requiring a joint Transformer forward pass, at the cost of a much larger index
It eliminates the need for any query-time computation whatsoever
It is a training technique for compressing cross-encoders into bi-encoders with no accuracy loss
explanation: ColBERT's document token vectors are computed and stored ahead of time, and MaxSim finds each query token's best-matching document token at query time — a genuine middle ground between bi-encoder speed and cross-encoder precision, paid for with a much larger multi-vector index.

promptText: Why is a reranker score of 0.6 from one provider (e.g., Cohere Rerank) not comparable to a score of 0.6 from a different reranker model (e.g., bge-reranker) for the same query-document pair?
options: Because reranker scores are only ever integers, never decimals

Different reranker models are trained on different data with different objectives and output calibration (raw logits vs. sigmoid-normalized probabilities), so only the relative ordering within a single reranking call for a single query is meaningful, not absolute cross-model comparison
Because Cohere and bge-reranker use fundamentally different definitions of relevance that cannot be reconciled
Because scores from different providers are always inversely correlated
explanation: Treating a 0.6 from one provider as equivalent to a 0.6 from another is a common and avoidable mistake, especially during vendor migrations — score scale is not standardized across reranker models.

promptText: What is 'position bias' in LLM-as-reranker prompting, and how does a sliding-window listwise strategy mitigate it?
options: Position bias means the LLM always ranks the shortest document first; sliding windows fix it by padding all documents to equal length

Position bias is the tendency of an LLM to favor candidates based on where they sit in the prompt (primacy/recency effects) rather than content; a sliding-window strategy reranks smaller overlapping sub-windows and merges results, limiting how much any single position in one giant prompt can dominate
Position bias only affects pointwise cross-encoders, never LLM-as-reranker approaches
Position bias is eliminated entirely by increasing the LLM's context window size
explanation: This is a failure mode specific to listwise LLM-as-reranker prompting with no equivalent in pointwise cross-encoders, which never see more than one candidate at a time and so cannot be influenced by list position.

promptText: Why are 'hard negatives' especially important for training an effective reranker, as opposed to random negatives?
options: Hard negatives are cheaper to obtain than random negatives

A hard negative is topically or lexically close to the query but not actually relevant, forcing the model to learn the fine-grained distinction between 'similar' and 'relevant' — the exact gap reranking exists to close; random negatives are trivially dissimilar and teach the model little about production failure modes
Hard negatives are only useful for training bi-encoders, not cross-encoders
Random negatives always produce better calibrated relevance scores than hard negatives
explanation: Training on random negatives alone teaches the model to reject easy cases it would already reject; hard negatives mirror the real production problem — documents that fool bi-encoder similarity but aren't truly relevant.

promptText: How should hybrid search (reciprocal rank fusion of dense and lexical retrieval) and reranking be ordered in a production RAG pipeline, and why does the order matter?
options: Rerank a narrow set first, then fuse in lexical results afterward, since reranking is more accurate and should run first

Fuse widely for recall first (hybrid search combining dense and lexical signals to maximize candidates in the pool), then rerank narrowly for precision second — reversing this order would mean reranking cannot recover candidates that fusion never included
The order never matters since both operations are commutative
Hybrid search and reranking should never be used together in the same pipeline
explanation: Hybrid search improves recall by combining complementary cheap signals at corpus scale; reranking operates strictly downstream to improve precision within whatever candidate set fusion already produced — this ordering is an architectural invariant.

promptText: A staff engineer proposes a three-stage funnel: wide retrieval (top-100) to a fast cross-encoder reranker (narrowing to top-15-20) to an LLM-as-judge for the final handful before generation. What is the strongest justification for this cascading design over using LLM-as-reranker directly on the wide candidate set?
options: LLM-as-judge is always more accurate than a cross-encoder regardless of candidate count, so it should replace the cross-encoder entirely

The cascade bounds the expensive LLM-as-judge's cost to a small, fixed shortlist regardless of the original retrieval width, capturing most of the recall protection of a wide candidate set and most of the ordering correction cheaply, while reserving the LLM's expensive contextual reasoning for only the few candidates where it matters most
Cross-encoders cannot process more than 20 candidates in a single API call under any circumstances
This design eliminates the need for an absolute relevance-score floor entirely
explanation: Running LLM-as-reranker prices across an entire wide candidate set (e.g., top-100) is far more expensive than a fast cross-encoder pass; the cascade generalizes the same cheap-and-wide, then narrower-and-more-expensive funnel principle to a third stage.

promptText: Why can distillation from a cross-encoder's relevance judgments actually improve first-stage bi-encoder retrieval quality, and does this eliminate the architectural need for a separate reranking stage?
options: It eliminates the need for reranking entirely, since a distilled bi-encoder becomes as accurate as a cross-encoder

The cross-encoder's fine-grained relevance judgments can be used as training signal to fine-tune the bi-encoder, teaching it to place truly relevant documents closer together in embedding space even without joint attention at inference time — this narrows the gap reranking needs to close but does not eliminate reranking's architectural necessity, since the underlying bi-encoder still can't perform joint query-document reasoning at inference time
Distillation only works in the reverse direction — from bi-encoders into cross-encoders — never the other way
This technique requires abandoning the two-stage retrieval architecture entirely
explanation: Retrieval and reranking form a closed feedback loop rather than two permanently independent stages, but the fundamental cost-model asymmetry (bi-encoders precomputable, cross-encoders not) still means reranking remains architecturally necessary even as distillation narrows the accuracy gap it needs to close.
